3 SGX Hidden Gems That Grew Profits by 24% (or More!)
article:
If you follow earnings season, you’ll know
blue chips
tend to hog the spotlight.
This time, some of the biggest profit gains came from much smaller companies.
Three Singapore-listed
small caps
grew their profits by 24% or more, and one more than doubled its bottom line.
If you invest for dividends, profit growth is a good start.
The cash behind it matters more.
One thing to keep in mind as you read: the three report over different periods, so watch the labels.
Can Tiong Woon keep raising its dividend?
Tiong Woon Corporation Holding Ltd
(SGX: BQM) is a one-stop integrated heavy-lift specialist with a presence in 12 countries.
Crane and transport hire makes up 96% of revenue.
For the financial year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), revenue rose 15% year on year (YoY) to S$187.7 million.
Profit attributable to shareholders climbed 24% to S$23.9 million.
The crane business drove the gains. Heavy Lift and Haulage external revenue grew 12% YoY, helped by Singapore, India and Brunei.
Gross margin widened to 40.7% from 37.6% on higher margins in that segment.
Turn to the cash flow statement, and you’ll see why Tiong Woon stands out.
Operating cash flow rose 31%, while capital expenditure nearly halved.
Free cash flow rose to S$43.7 million from S$6.3 million a year ago.
The board shared some of that cash.
It proposed a final dividend of S$0.025 per share, up 43% from S$0.0175.
You’ll still want to keep an eye on the balance sheet.
Tiong Woon held S$86.6 million in cash and bank deposits against S$108.0 million in borrowings, excluding lease liabilities.
The low capex bill may not last either. Management plans to keep renewing and expanding its fleet.
Demand looks supportive.
Tiong Woon cites official forecasts of Singapore construction demand of S$47 billion to S$53 billion in 2026, with Changi Airport Terminal 5 among the big projects.
Can Micro-Mechanics turn record profits into bigger dividends?
Micro-Mechanics (Holdings) Ltd
(SGX: 5DD) makes precision tools and parts used in semiconductor manufacturing.
For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (1QFY2027) ended 30 September 2026, revenue rose 45.0% YoY to S$24.2 million, an all-time quarterly high.
Net profit rose 102.8% to S$6.4 million, also a quarterly record.
Wondering why profit grew faster than sales?
Look at the margins.
Gross margin widened to a 20-quarter high of 55.0%, from 51.5% a year ago.
Overheads fell to 20.7% of revenue from 25.1%.
In other words, more of each extra dollar of sales now reaches the bottom line.
Free cash flow moved the other way.
It fell 10.6% YoY to S$3.7 million.
Trade receivables rose in line with higher revenue, and the company paid more tax.
Capital expenditure also rose to S$0.9 million from S$0.3 million.
Should that worry you? Not much.
Micro-Mechanics had S$33.3 million in cash and no bank borrowings as at 30 September 2026.
No dividend was declared for the quarter, and that is normal since the company typically declares dividends in the second and fourth quarters.
Spending is the bigger question.
Micro-Mechanics expects to invest S$12 million in FY2027, including expanding its manufacturing footprint.
Under a five-year strategy, it wants to double revenue to at least S$150 million. That investment will compete with dividends for cash.
What’s missing from Civmec’s record quarter?
Civmec Limited
(SGX: P9D) is an integrated construction and engineering services provider to the energy, resources, infrastructure, and marine and defence sectors.
It is headquartered in Henderson, Western Australia and reports in Australian dollars.
For the first quarter of the fiscal year ending 30 June 2027 (1QFY2027), revenue rose 70.2% YoY to a record A$324 million.
Net profit after tax climbed 75.2% to A$18.4 million.
A significant uplift in activity in Civmec’s construction division drove the growth.
Work ramped up on BHP’s Port Debottlenecking Project 2 and Iluka Resources’ Eneabba Rare Earths Refinery.
The order book stood at around A$1.4 billion, up from A$1.15 billion a year ago.
Here’s the thing: the quarterly update did not include a cash flow statement or balance sheet.
You can’t see free cash flow, cash or debt for the quarter.
For a contractor, profit and cash can drift apart as big projects ramp up, so this is a real gap.
You should also note how thin the margins are.
Civmec’s net profit margin was 5.7%, against 5.5% a year ago.
That leaves little room for error on large projects.
No dividend was declared for the quarter.
Civmec paid a final dividend of A$0.035 on 23 October 2026.
Together with the A$0.025 interim, that took FY2026 dividends to A$0.060.
Get Smart: Check whether the cash followed the profit
Free cash flow
is the lifeblood of dividends.
So when a company posts a big profit gain, ask one more question: did the cash show up too?
Tiong Woon passes that test.
Profit grew 24%, while free cash flow rose almost sevenfold.
Micro-Mechanics doubled its profit, but free cash flow dipped as it invested more and waited on customer payments.
Civmec hasn’t shown its cash yet.
So the next time a small cap reports a record, open the cash flow statement before you get excited.
Profit that never turns into cash shouldn’t count for much in your dividend plans.

title: Singapore extends GST-exemption to activities related to wholesale gold transactions
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Ministry of Finance (MOF) will be extending the GST waiver to specified wholesale investment precious metal (IPM) related services between institutional participants covered by the existing GST framework. These services include activities such as vaulting, refining/recasting, assaying, and broking.

The initiative seeks to support the growth of wholesale Loco Singapore gold market activities where the gold traded is not for domestic consumption. This new tax framework is expected to take effect from April 2027, with further details to be announced at Budget 2027.

Under the current Approved Refiner and Consolidator Scheme, GST is waived on IPM-related goods supplied between approved refiners and consolidators for refining activities, to ease their cashflow and compliance.The existing framework also exempts the import and local supply of IPM from GST.

Deputy prime minister and MAS chairman Gan Kim Yong thinks the new GST framework will both facilitate the trading of gold and central bank storage of gold in Singapore. He adds: “I have to emphasise that this is a transaction between institutions and the wholesale trade, and it's not targeted at the consumer retail market. So that is why the GST framework is built on that basis.”

Speaking at a media doorstop, Gan also announced that MAS is launching its central bank gold vaulting service. “Given an increasingly uncertain external environment, demand for gold as an asset class is rising as investors and central banks look for resilience and diversification,” says Gan. “Foreign central banks and sovereign entities now have an additional sovereign custody option in Singapore for their gold reserves.”

Besides offering an alternative storage option, the service also provides secure, allocated custody, reliable servicing and efficient access to gold-market liquidity during Asian trading hours, notes MAS.

See also: Central banks buy gold at fastest pace since 2024, WGC says

Under this development, MAS will store up to 500 tonnes of gold in its national currency vault, with room for expansion as demand grows. MAS will also offer gold custody accounts to select Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise and experience in providing gold-related services and trading liquidity to these institutions.

Gan says that the development of Singapore’s gold market is a “natural extension” to Singapore’s role as a trusted financial centre and will anchor new high-value activities across trading, risk management, custody, and professional services in the city-state.

“By connecting secure storage with trading and settlement, we are building a market where gold can be held, managed and traded in Singapore,” he adds. “It will create good jobs and capabilities, while adding depth and resilience to our financial sector, strengthening Singapore’s role as a trusted connector between Asia and global gold markets.”

See also: Gold climbs back from one-year low as dip buyers arrest slide

Gan also shared that Singapore’s gold clearing system will be ready by end-2026, with live trading and liquidity building up from the first quarter next year. In June, DBS, Deutsche Bank, ICBC Standard Bank, JP Morgan, OCBC, and UOB signed a memorandum of understanding with SGX Group to develop an over-the-counter gold clearing system,

MAS announced that industry testing of the clearing system has been completed and the clearing system rulebook will be finalised soon. Live trading and market operations are expected to commence in 1Q 2027, with gold market liquidity building throughout the year.

JP Morgan senior country officer Wai Mei Hong says, “We are pleased to work with SGX Group in advancing Singapore’s OTC gold clearing system. As global demand for gold grows, this initiative will strengthen Singapore’s role as a trading hub, deepen liquidity across time zones and help us better serve clients.”

UOB head of group global markets Kelvin Ng says that the combination of vaulting, enhanced tax support for wholesale gold activities and a gold clearing ecosystem will create "stronger foundations" for market growth. “These developments will deepen liquidity, improve price discovery and reinforce Singapore's role as a key precious metals centre serving the Asia-Pacific region,” adds Ng.

In addition, it was also announced that SGX is targeting to launch its physically deliverable gold kilobar futures in the second quarter of 2027.

title: Australia to create AI safety regulator, mandatory safety rules
article:
(Nov 10): Australia will create a new artificial intelligence (AI) safety regulator that will have the power to impose “significant penalties” on companies that do the wrong thing, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday in Canberra.

The government is in the process of writing AI-related legislation, with the new regulator to be included in those bills, Albanese said at a press conference. Firms will need to provide mandatory notifications of any security incidents to the government and allow independent evaluation of their models, he added.

The issue of AI safety was brought to the fore in September when it was revealed that an OpenAI model had hacked an Australian government website. While the information accessed wasn’t sensitive personal data, the attack on a government website shone a spotlight on such risks.

That followed a series of incidents in which OpenAI models broke into online resources of outside companies, most notably with the case of Hugging Face, a website hosting AI datasets.

Australia established a review in response to the hacking. It recommended changes including reforming criminal laws so that the government can criminally punish “egregious regulatory non-compliance” and create a “failure to prevent” offence where a company creates a model and doesn’t take reasonable steps to stop it from doing harm.

The government will accept all of the review’s recommendations, Albanese said.

See also: Why Singapore's next AI question is value, not just spend

title: Singapore’s interbank rate hits highest in more than a year
article:
(Nov 10): Singapore’s benchmark interest rate climbed to the highest level in more than a year on tighter local liquidity and expectations for further US interest-rate hikes.

The cost of overnight borrowing in Singapore’s interbank market rose 11.7 basis points to 1.7446% as of Friday, according to data published Tuesday. That was the highest since July 2025. Local markets were shut on Monday for a holiday.

Singapore’s borrowing costs are largely influenced by global interest rates and currency expectations because the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts monetary policy through the exchange rate. That leaves local rates sensitive to shifts in US monetary policy, with markets bracing for the possibility of further Federal Reserve tightening after a 25-basis-point hike in September.

Liquidity in Singapore has also tightened as loan growth outpaced deposits. The loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 69.8% in September, the highest since August 2024, from 65.8% at the end of last year, according to the latest central bank data.

“Liquidity appears on the tight side recently, while the long weekend might have added to the tightness,” said Frances Cheung, head of foreign exchange and rates strategy at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp.

See also: ‘Longer-term measures’ being studied to strengthen transparency, trust in real estate industry: Sun Xueling

Cheung said compounded SORA rates, while lagging, “provide a better picture of the broader trend”. The three-month rate is moving towards around 1.4%, in line with her long-held expectation for around year-end, she said.

The three-month compounded SORA was at 1.3413% on Friday.

title: Nvidia intervened in US probe of Megaspeed chip smuggling
article:
(Nov 10): Nvidia Corp’s general counsel intervened in a US government probe of suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, questioning whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining an executive from the Singapore-based firm who’s now at the heart of a scandal threatening Jensen Huang.

In late summer 2025, Nvidia’s Tim Teter called Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees US chip export curbs, to ask about the Megaspeed investigation, according to people familiar with the matter.

Specifically, Teter wanted to know whether Kessler’s Bureau of Industry and Security was involved in the Singapore government’s recent detention of Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, according to the people. Singapore police had brought Alice in for questioning and restricted her from leaving the country. BIS was not involved in that action, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity owing to the sensitivity of the matter.

Jensen on Sunday admitted to having an affair with Alice after previously lying about the nature of their relationship, which is now the subject of an investigation by Nvidia’s board. An Nvidia spokesperson said that Teter was unaware of the affair at the time he called Kessler about Alice’s detention in Singapore.

It’s unclear whether Teter made any specific requests of Kessler related to his agency’s investigation into Megaspeed, which was separate from Singapore’s. But in the weeks that followed, BIS staff were muzzled in their ability to look into the company, including a mandate that they route all requests of Nvidia through Kessler or seek his approval for outreach — a highly unusual step that remains unique to the chipmaker, the people said. They were also told not to mention Megaspeed or Speedmatrix, the company’s Malaysian subsidiary, in external communications.

Teter, meanwhile, reached out directly to the agency’s staff, including requesting a meeting with one of them, according to some of the people. That BIS employee declined the meeting, and Teter responded that he didn’t understand why his request was spurned, since Kessler had granted him permission to communicate with BIS employees. It’s unclear exactly what Teter wanted to discuss with these individuals.

See also: Nvidia shares drop after CEO Huang’s affair triggers board probe

The employees forwarded the email to Kessler, who told them hours later to continue handling the case by the book, to which the employees responded: “10-4. Thank you.” Kessler didn’t otherwise weigh in on how the employees should proceed with the case, according to one of the people. The New York Times reported earlier on Teter’s outreach to BIS employees and their exchange with Kessler.

“BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a spokesperson for the agency said. “BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high.”

In late 2025, the Justice Department, which was working on the case with BIS — standard practice for any BIS investigation that turns into a criminal probe — requested that BIS pause its efforts, the people said. BIS has not made any progress since then, despite the agency having enough evidence to move forward.

See also: Anthropic buys power for AI data centres in US$3.4 bil deal, FT says

It’s an extraordinary episode that raises questions about Nvidia’s ability to influence US investigations into breaches of China chip curbs, as well as what exactly Teter sought to do with any additional information about Alice’s detention in Singapore.

An Nvidia spokesperson, asked about the company’s intervention in BIS’s Megaspeed probe, said that Nvidia consults with government officials “to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups.”

“We work to resolve any allegations of ‘diversion’ promptly, to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide,” the spokesperson said. “Unresolved questions about lawful business undercut longstanding US policy and hurt American economic and national security.”

Despite that stance, in the months after Teter’s initial call with Kessler, Nvidia gave BIS an incomplete account of its business with Megaspeed. After several visits to Megaspeed’s data centers — 12 facilities owned by eight companies across three countries in Southeast Asia — Nvidia had sent inventory checks to the agency and declared to Bloomberg News in mid-November 2025 that everything was where it should be.

The company also said at the time that it had asked the US government whether it needed to cut off business with Megaspeed, and was told no.

But Nvidia’s tabulations, as relayed to the US government, undercounted the number of chips it had sold to Megaspeed via hardware partners by 50,000 units, according to trade records analysed by Bloomberg. That’s worth billions of dollars. After being pressed about the gap, Nvidia told Bloomberg in December 2025 that it had checked additional Megaspeed warehouses that contained the missing hardware, while declining to state exactly how many chips it found in those facilities or provide any further details.

Nvidia also declined to comment on significant additional discrepancies in Megaspeed’s data centre footprint, including that two of the eight data centre operators Nvidia told officials in Washington it had visited said they did not, in fact, have Megaspeed’s hardware — and that Megaspeed boasts something of a Chinese corporate twin. It’s unclear whether Nvidia has communicated with BIS or DOJ on these topics.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Since then, the largest of Megaspeed’s data centre landlords dropped Megaspeed as a tenant. Nvidia, for its part, has consistently declined to comment on whether it has completed any additional visits to that site or any of Megaspeed’s other facilities, despite pledging to do so nearly a year ago.

BIS, meanwhile, has declined to impose restrictions on Nvidia’s ability to do business with the firm despite calls for such a step from senior levels of the Trump administration. Megaspeed has categorically denied the chip diversion allegations, and said that its outreach to the US government about the probe has gone unanswered.

The company added that Singapore’s investigation “into activities related to alleged chip diversion concluded earlier this year with no adverse action against Megaspeed.” Bloomberg has been unable to reach Alice Huang despite repeated attempts over the past year. Megaspeed was not speaking on her behalf.

Around three months ago, Nvidia’s Teter had a call with someone else on Trump’s team — an official at the White House. He told this official, according to a person familiar with the call, that Alice is not as important in Megaspeed as she makes herself out to be, a likely reference to her statement on LinkedIn that she is the company’s CEO even though she doesn’t hold and has never held that role on paper. Still, because of the bad publicity surrounding Alice, Teter continued, Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed.

That bad publicity began in October 2025, when The New York Times first reported that the US government was looking into the company. In November 2025, Malaysian trade records show, Megaspeed imported at least 17,544 of Nvidia’s GB300s processors, at the time the most advanced and sought after AI chips on the market, worth some US$787 million.

Today, Megaspeed remains an official Nvidia Cloud Partner — a coveted designation in the data centre world that Nvidia generally takes away from companies when they no longer do business with those firms.

title: Oil extends drop as Trump says further Iran strikes unnecessary
article:
(Nov 10): Oil extended declines from the lowest close since August after US President Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran wouldn’t be necessary.

Brent dropped below US$92 a barrel after sliding almost 6% on Monday, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$86. Hopes for an earlier end to the war with Iran have grown since the US midterm elections, with congressional Democrats weighing whether to use a Dec 11 government shutdown deadline to pressure Trump to end the conflict, now in its ninth month.

The president said the US remains “locked and loaded”, while signalling he’s looking to wind down the conflict after the midterm results underscored its unpopularity. “Iran, militarily, is effectively over,” he told reporters on Monday after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House. Qatar is a mediator in talks between the US and Iran.

Brent has tumbled from a six-month high at the end of October. Last week, the global benchmark notched its biggest weekly decline since April 2020 when not adjusted for expiry. However, it’s not yet clear whether the softer rhetoric will translate into tangible progress towards ending the war started by the US and Israel, with political uncertainty deepening after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lost his parliamentary majority at the end of last month.

“The midterm results have significantly narrowed Trump’s options for a large-scale, long-term military operation against Iran and that’s reflected in his rhetoric,” said Takahiro Asaoka, senior economist at Itochu Research Institute Inc. That’s taking some of the geopolitical premium out of oil, although Brent will likely stay above US$85 a barrel without a deal with Tehran, he added.

Months of on-and-off negotiations have failed to produce a resolution. Tehran has insisted that the US end its naval blockade of the country’s ports and lift sanctions, while Washington is pressing Iran to stop attacking vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and make concessions over its nuclear programme.

See also: Oil extends rebound on uncertainty over Iran war peace progress

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down the chances of a breakthrough in talks with Iran, while risks to energy infrastructure remain. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline was targeted Monday in the Medina region, causing a limited fire that was extinguished, the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported.

Geopolitical risks elsewhere also remain in focus. Ukraine continued to strike Russian refineries, while Moscow repeatedly targeted energy and civilian infrastructure in its neighbour. US-mediated talks between the sides are due to start Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, and the presence of higher-level diplomats than in previous rounds has been seen as a sign of greater openness to substantive negotiations after months of stalemate.

Traders this week will also watch monthly market reports from all three major forecasting agencies: the US Energy Information Administration on Tuesday, Opec on Wednesday and the International Energy Agency on Friday.

See also: Oil extends slide after plunging 8% on hopes to end US-Iran war
• Brent for January settlement dropped 0.8% to US$91.80 a barrel at 9.58am in Singapore.

title: Asian stocks climb as tech rallies, oil slips
article:
(Nov 10): Asian stocks advanced, tracking Wall Street higher as a rally in technology shares and a further decline in oil prices boosted risk sentiment.

South Korea’s Kospi Index jumped 3.9% to lead gains in the region, followed by Japan’s Nikkei 225 and Taiwan’s benchmark. A broader gauge of Asian equities climbed 2%, while futures for US benchmarks were little changed.

On Monday, the S&P 500 rallied the most since April 8. A gauge of chipmakers surged nearly 7% while the Nasdaq 100 ended 3.4% higher. That came even as shares of Nvidia Corp slid 4.3% amid a probe into chief executive officer Jensen Huang after his admission of an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy.

Elsewhere, Brent crude slipped further on Tuesday after slumping almost 6% to settle below US$93 a barrel in the previous session. President Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran wouldn’t be necessary but the US remains “locked and loaded”, an indication that he’s winding down the conflict.

The rally in stocks follows a tumultuous week during which chipmakers were sold off on concerns that the Democratic sweep of US Congress in the midterms would spur tighter regulation of the artificial intelligence industry. Meanwhile, a steady decline in oil has helped temper inflation fears.

“The sharp drop in oil prices has given markets some much-needed breathing room,” said Dilin Wu, a strategist at Pepperstone Group. “Investors are also buying back into stocks after last week’s brutal selloff. We still need to see whether buying interest can hold up.”

See also: Asia hedge funds, rich investors face big losses in AI rout

Anthropic PBC can begin formally marketing its much-anticipated IPO as early as Tuesday, enabling it to make the case to investors that now is the right time to go public despite last week’s swoon in AI-related stocks.

The recent tech selloff represented a reset rather than the start of a structural downturn in the AI investment cycle. But the rebound does not remove the risks created by concentrated positioning and elevated expectations, said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office.

On the economic front, investors will be watching October US consumer prices data, which is slated to be released Tuesday and is expected to show smaller increases than in September.

See also: Watch for the double top pattern that precedes a market crash

“We continue to see economic conditions as supportive of corporate fundamentals,” said Brock Weimer at Edward Jones. “Thus, we recommend that investors maintain an overweight allocation to equities relative to fixed income.”
• Nvidia Corp’s general counsel intervened in a US government probe of suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, questioning whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining an executive from the Singapore-based firm who’s now at the heart of a scandal threatening Jensen Huang.
• Honda Motor Co plans to build a US$3 billion ($3.8 billion) factory in central Ohio to manufacture its next-generation hybrids, boosting its output capacity for the popular vehicles.
• Alphabet Inc’s Google is rolling out a broader array of AI chips, aiming to capitalise on its rapid ascent as a challenger to Nvidia in a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
• Boeing Co will cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce after delaying production increases, the US planemaker’s first job reduction in nearly two years and a sign that its turnaround is far from complete.

title: Canada expands US tariff exemptions, cuts some aluminium relief
article:
(Nov 10): Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is changing the rules for importers, allowing them to apply for exemptions from Canadian tariffs on a wider range of US goods while ending relief on some American-made aluminum products.

When US President Donald Trump began imposing tariffs on Canadian goods in March 2025, Canada responded with retaliatory levies. But Carney’s government allowed importers to request “remission” from the tariffs in some circumstances — for example, if they’re buying essential products from the US that are hard to find elsewhere.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Monday the government will now extend tariff relief for “non-steel goods” made in the US and used in Canadian mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction, as well as some other items.

Companies in those categories will be eligible for tariff remission until June 30, 2028.

The remission program is already so broad that most of the counter-tariffs Canada applies on US shipments haven’t actually resulted in revenue for the government.

From March 2025 through October 26, 2026, Canada assessed C$14.1 billion (US$10 billion) worth of tariffs on products from the US. But C$8.9 billion was “remitted or relieved” to mitigate the hit to Canada, leaving net revenue of C$5.2 billion, according to a disclosure last week by the government.

See also: Vietnam turns to taxes, state borrowing to finance growth push

Products used by some public health, education, safety and national security organizations also will be exempt from tariffs until June 2028, the government said Monday.

At the same time, Champagne also announced the end of tariff remission on a list of other products to encourage purchases from Canadian manufacturers.

Tariff relief will no longer be available on some US-made trailers as of Dec 1, nor on types of aluminum wire, pipes, tubes, or some paperboard products, from Feb 1, 2027. That’s “to incentivize the use of domestic inputs,” the Department of Finance said in a statement.

See also: Asia’s innovation capacity is improving but could be better

Canada doubled counter-tariffs on many US aluminium products to 50% on Sept 8, while still allowing Canadian buyers to request relief. Some Canadian aluminium manufacturers, already facing export challenges due to hefty US duties, have said that the remission programme leaves them at a disadvantage in pursuing domestic sales.

“By adjusting our tariff relief measures, we are helping our businesses staying competitive, encouraging the use of Canadian-made goods, and protecting our industries and workers most impacted by the unfair US tariffs,” Champagne said in the statement.
